articles.title: Brazil’s left reinvented the right’s online playbook. It helped Lula win
articles.summary: For three weeks in October, Veridiana Cunha became a so-called “soldier” for a digital army fighting to reelect Brazil’s leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
articles.body: For three weeks in October, Veridiana Cunha became a so-called “soldier” for a digital army fighting to reelect Brazil’s leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Every few minutes, the 48-year-old would interrupt her day job in São Paulo as a copy editor and check WhatsApp for new instructions. She even reactivated an Instagram account she hadn’t used since 2022 and learned how to post on X for the first time for the cause. “I’d edit a text, then go to the army. Edit another text, then go to the army,” she told CNN of a WhatsApp channel, led by Congressman André Janones, that became a virtual campaign headquarters during the final weeks of Brazil’s presidential campaign. Cunha was one of millions of Brazilians who joined the channel called “Lula’s Army.” Their mission: to reverse Lula’s first-round defeat on October 4 to the right-wing senator Flávio Bolsonaro, scion of former President Jair Bolsonaro. And they succeeded. Lula won the election on October 25, which analysts partly attribute to the eleventh-hour strategy of harnessing a digital playbook long associated with Brazil’s right of using WhatsApp to amplify political messaging and mobilize voters. From coordinated social media campaigns to reclaiming national symbols, the online strategy mobilized many to vote for Lula, in an effort that experts say offers a striking example of how the Brazilian left learned to fight the right on its turf. Millions of “soldiers,” one command WhatsApp is a powerful force in Brazilian politics. Jair Bolsonaro’s successful presidential campaign in 2018 was supported by extensive networks of private groups that spread videos, political messages and disinformation. But ahead of the October 4, first-round vote, Lula’s campaign had struggled to compete with the right’s digital operation. While Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign had long made social media a central part of its strategy, Lula’s team underestimated its importance, according to Lucas Fernandes, a political analyst at BMJ Consultores Associados. “The right understood this and applied it on several fronts, not just to Flávio’s candidacy, while the left failed to make that transition,” Fernandes said, highlighting social media as one of the key factors for Flávio’s victory in the first round. That changed after Lula’s defeat when Janones, 42, emerged as a central figure in this new playbook. The congressman for the state of Minas Gerais created the WhatsApp channel in April. After Lula’s first-round loss to Bolsonaro, Janones transformed it into a virtual command center, issuing coordinated instructions to supporters who were suddenly confronting the possibility of losing the presidency. Viktor Chagas, a professor at Fluminense Federal University who researches political communication, described Janones as a politician who “fights the far right with the same resources it uses,” resorting to emotionally charged messages, aggressive language and, at times, content of dubious origin. It was a strategy he deployed on the channel, which saw it swell from 50,000 followers before the first-round vote to nearly 11 million in three weeks as Janones rallied supporters to help Lula stage a historic comeback. From anti-system figure to digital general of Lula Within Congress, Janones is known for his combative style, which he dubbed “cultural Janonism,” adopting tactics associated with Bolsonarism, according to Chagas. This included provocative language, emotionally charged posts, and attacks on his adversaries. It also turned Janones into a polarizing figure, who last year was suspended by Congress for three months for offensive statements against another combative lawmaker, the right-wing politician Nikolas Ferreira. Through videos, audio messages and social media posts, Janones instructed his followers to promote hashtags, comment on livestreams, share videos, like posts, publish photos making the “L” hand gesture in support of Lula, and recruit new members. He called for a panelaço — a traditional Brazilian form of protest in which people bang pots and pans — during Flávio Bolsonaro’s highly anticipated interview on TV Globo, as a way to boycott the broadcast. Janones also urged supporters to avoid commenting on opponents’ posts, warning that engaging with their content could inadvertently boost its visibility through social media algorithms. The pace was so intense that Janones went so far as to condemn resting unless the “soldier” could find a replacement for the “missions.” On October 17, he wrote on the channel: “If there is a substitute soldier, the change is authorized. Pass him the cell phone. Rest and come back in ten minutes.” Chagas described the strategy as a form of “gamification,” which fostered a sense of collective purpose. According to the academic, that structure gave progressive digital activism a level of coordination that had been absent even during Lula’s successful campaign in 2022. Bolsonaro’s strategy focused on disseminating content from a few major influencers, while “Lula’s Army” had a centralized command that instructed its members to create and disseminate their own content as well as official lines. Janones not only told them what to share but taught them how to do it, experts noted. Leonardo Magalhães Firmino, chief executive of research firm IPSE Global, compared the method to training thousands of small social media managers. But the rise in online activity also raised concerns about misinformation. In one widely circulated image by the left, Brazilian soccer legend Ronaldo appears to be wearing a national team jersey bearing Lula’s ballot number, 13, and making the “L” gesture. The image was manipulated by artificial intelligence and posted by a Colombian artist, according to Brazilian fact-checking outlet Agência Lupa. Ronaldo’s representatives said it had been used without his authorization. While Janones’ tactics tend to pursue democratic ends, Chagas argues that they could also degrade public debate by reducing complex political discussions to a constant confrontation. CNN reached out to Janones, who has previously denied spreading disinformation, for comment. On the channel, Janones called himself “general,” assigned daily “missions” to Lula’s supporters, and urged them to take the campaign beyond their own social media. The tactics frustrated Bolsonaro’s supporters. On October 11, a supreme court judge ordered the suspension of the WhatsApp group following a complaint by Bolsonaro’s campaign for alleged disinformation. The decision was later overturned. Did the “army” change the outcome of the election? Lula’s victory was decided by factors beyond the digital battle: electoral participation, the redistribution of votes from eliminated candidates, and geographical changes in support for candidates. But Janones’ online mobilization was fundamental to Lula’s victory, says Firmino. “I have no doubt. Without that, I don’t think the comeback would have happened,” he told CNN. “He organized the militancy, he gave them a method. I think that’s the main point.” According to Firmino, the right underestimated Janones’ strategy, saying that he only spoke with Lula supporters. But that was the point: the goal was to speak directly with the “soldiers” who were already converted, not the undecided. The “soldiers” were the ones who would take the message beyond the channel and to their family, friends, undecided voters, and those thinking about abstaining, he said. ‘I managed to change a vote’ For Cunha, the missions meant much more than a political cause. Her mother, a longtime Lula supporter, became seriously ill in August and she spent weeks by her side in the Brazilian state of Minas Gerais, so she did not vote in the first round. Back in São Paulo for work, she needed a distraction and a purpose, which she found in digital mobilization. “The Army saved Brazil, it saved Lula and it saved me a little too,” she said. Participating in the campaign allowed her to feel closer to her mother and continue fighting for a cause they both shared. But one of her greatest satisfactions came on election day, when a friend, who was thinking of abstaining, finally went to the polls and voted for Lula. “I managed to change a vote,” Cunha said. No one can determine how many stories like hers translated into additional votes on a national scale. But for Cunha, the victory had an unexpected consequence: After three weeks spent almost entirely campaigning, getting back to normal proved harder than she imagined. “I think we’re living through a kind of post-traumatic stress from the Army, like we’ve really gone to war,” she said. “We’re exhausted, but we want more missions. We feel like we can conquer the world.”

articles.title: Travis Scott's Cactus Jack Foundation partners with a fashion scholarship fund to award students $10,000 each and offer hands-on design training to build practical skills
articles.summary: Travis Scott's Cactus Jack Foundation has partnered with the Fashion Scholarship Fund (FSF) to support aspiring fashion designers through scholarships,
articles.body: Travis Scott's Cactus Jack Foundation has partnered with the Fashion Scholarship Fund (FSF) to support aspiring fashion designers through scholarships, mentorship and practical design training. The collaboration, known as the Cactus Jack Design Ethos 101 programme, offers selected students $10,000 each and access to an online curriculum developed by the Cactus Jack team and its partners. Participants also get the opportunity to take part in immersive learning experiences at the Cact.us Design Center in Houston, Texas. The initiative aims to introduce emerging creatives to the ideas and processes behind Scott's brand, exploring the intersection of fashion, design and music. The partnership has continued across multiple scholarship cohorts, with three new Cactus Jack Design Ethos scholars announced in March 2026.Travis Scott's foundation expands fashion education opportunitiesScott's foundation launched the Cactus Jack Design Ethos 101 programme in partnership with the Fashion Scholarship Fund as part of a broader effort to create educational opportunities for aspiring creatives.The programme combines financial support with learning opportunities designed to help students explore fashion and design beyond conventional classroom instruction. Its online curriculum is developed by the Cactus Jack team and its partners, while selected scholars receive mentorship and opportunities for immersive experiences at the Cact.us Design Center.Scott said the initiative was intended to help aspiring creatives explore fashion, design and music while encouraging them to develop their own ideas.Peter Arnold, executive director of the Fashion Scholarship Fund, said the partnership would provide the organisation's network of alumni, current scholars and applicants with access to creative resources, mentors and career development opportunities.Three students named Cactus Jack scholars in 2026The Cactus Jack Foundation announced three new scholarship recipients at the Fashion Scholarship Fund's annual gala in New York on March 24, 2026.The recipients were Cameroun Blount of North Carolina A&T State University, Caira Coleman of Spelman College and Jasmine Cox of the Savannah College of Art and Design.Scott introduced the scholars at the event, which celebrated recipients from the Fashion Scholarship Fund and the Virgil Abloh "Post-Modern" Scholarship programme, alongside other figures from the fashion and creative industries.The three students joined an initiative that had already supported scholars from earlier cohorts. According to the Fashion Scholarship Fund's announcement, three students from the Class of 2024 received Cactus Jack Design Ethos scholarships, followed by three recipients from the Class of 2025.Each selected Cactus Jack scholar receives a $10,000 award. Across the three cohorts announced for 2024, 2025 and 2026, the nine identified recipients represent $90,000 in scholarship awards.What students learn through Design Ethos 101The programme is designed to immerse students in the creative world behind Scott's Cactus Jack brand, with a focus on fashion, design and music.Its online educational component features a curriculum created by the Cactus Jack team and its partners. The initiative also includes mentorship and opportunities for selected scholars to participate in hands-on workshops at the Cact.us Design Center in Houston.The foundation says the programme encourages independent thinking and introduces participants to real-world applications of creative concepts, with industry experts guiding them through topics related to design, fashion and music.The practical component gives students an opportunity to engage with design processes in a professional creative environment. However, the programme's published details do not establish that every participant receives a formal internship or guaranteed employment with the Cactus Jack team.Inside the Cact.us Design Center in HoustonThe Cact.us Design Center is a youth-focused educational facility established by the Cactus Jack Foundation in partnership with TXRX Labs. It opened on November 3, 2021, in Houston, Texas.According to the foundation, the centre provides access to design education, technical training and mentorship for young people. Its facilities support a range of creative and manufacturing disciplines, including graphic design, fashion design, sneaker design, 3D printing, woodworking, laser cutting and fabrication.The centre also hosts programmes intended to help students develop practical skills and explore potential pathways to further education and careers.For the Design Ethos 101 partnership, the centre provides a physical setting where selected scholars can participate in immersive workshops and engage with the creative processes behind the Cactus Jack brand.The foundation's wider educational work includes the Cact.us Sneaker Lab, a design-focused programme that introduces young people in the Houston area to design-led fabrication and manufacturing.Fashion Scholarship Fund's role in the partnershipThe Fashion Scholarship Fund is a nonprofit organisation that supports students pursuing careers in fashion and related industries through scholarships, mentorship and career development opportunities.Its programmes connect students with educational resources and industry professionals. The organisation also administers the Virgil Abloh "Post-Modern" Scholarship programme, which supports aspiring creatives pursuing opportunities in fashion.The partnership with Cactus Jack expands the fund's network of educational initiatives by introducing students to the relationship between fashion, music and creative brand development.Peter Arnold, the fund's executive director, said the collaboration would give its community access to additional mentors, career development resources and educational opportunities.The partnership therefore combines the Fashion Scholarship Fund's established student network with the Cactus Jack Foundation's creative resources and design facilities.Cactus Jack Foundation's wider educational initiativesThe fashion scholarship programme is part of the foundation's broader work supporting education and skills development.Another initiative is the Waymon Webster HBCU Scholarship, named after Scott's grandfather, who was an alumnus and dean of Prairie View A&M University's graduate school. The programme helps students attending historically Black colleges and universities (HBCUs) who face financial difficulties that could prevent them from graduating on time.The foundation has also established Cactus Jack Gardens, a community initiative that works with elementary schools in Houston to introduce students to gardening, agricultural economics and nutrition.In addition, its partnership with Space Center Houston supports STEM education for Houston Independent School District students. The programme brings students together with educators and NASA engineers to work on design, coding and fabrication projects.What the scholarship programme offersThe Cactus Jack Design Ethos 101 partnership combines financial assistance with access to creative education and practical learning opportunities. Selected scholars receive $10,000 each, mentorship and opportunities to participate in workshops at the Cact.us Design Center.The programme also introduces aspiring designers to the creative thinking behind a brand associated with music and fashion, giving them an opportunity to explore how these industries intersect.The foundation and the Fashion Scholarship Fund have continued the partnership across multiple cohorts, with three new scholars announced in 2026.You use AI every day. articles.title: Mother fights to save Leicester leisure centre pool as council considers closure, warning her severely disabled son could lose his only accessible swimming facility
articles.summary: A mother in Leicester is urging the city council to keep New Parks Leisure Centre open, warning that its closure could leave her severely disabled son
articles.body: A mother in Leicester is urging the city council to keep New Parks Leisure Centre open, warning that its closure could leave her severely disabled son without access to a suitable swimming pool. Susan Wilder, 67, said the centre was the only facility she had found that could accommodate her 19-year-old son, who uses a wheelchair full-time and has complex physical, visual and hearing impairments.According to the BBC, swimming provides him with his only form of cardiovascular exercise and gives him a sense of freedom. Leicester City Council is consulting on proposals to close the leisure centre and invest £8 million in transforming Leicester Leys Leisure Centre.What makes pool facilities essential for Susan Wilder’s sonWilder said her son had been swimming at New Parks Leisure Centre for 19 years. He attends once one week and twice the next. She explained that he cannot use a standard pool chair because of his complex disabilities and requires specialist facilities to enter the water safely.He requires a poolside changing room with a ceiling-track hoist and a changing bed. The bed is brought to the poolside before he is transferred into the water using the hoist.Wilder said, "He loves the freedom of it and it's also the only cardiovascular exercise he gets.”"He has no speech, but he just generally loves the water."Family struggles to find an accessible swimming pool for disabled sonWilder said her family had searched for alternative swimming facilities, including centres outside Leicestershire, but had been unable to find a suitable option for her son.Wilder said, "We're willing to travel with him, we're willing to travel out of the county, but there's nowhere available to meet his needs.”She explained that while many disabled people could use swimming pools with the help of a pool chair, her son's needs were different. He requires facilities that allow him to be transferred from his changing bed into the water using a ceiling-track hoist.She said, "You have to look at people's needs to be able to access a swimming pool in the correct way. It's not just for my son, it's for anybody that has the disabilities that he's got.”New Parks closure plan sparks concern over disabled son's swimming accessLeicester City Council has described New Parks as the city's least used leisure centre and plans to spend £8 million transforming Leicester Leys Leisure Centre under the proposals.A petition calling for New Parks to be saved has received more than 2,150 signatures. However, Wilder said Leicester Leys would be too busy for her son because of his multi-sensory impairment, which includes hearing and visual impairments. She said he would not be able to swim there even if a pool hoist were installed.Wilder also expressed concern that the future of New Parks might already have been decided.According to Leicester Mercury, she said, “It’s a dif­fer­ent feel­ing; it’s sens­ory and helps relax him. I just want to make the coun­cil under­stand how import­ant it is that he and oth­ers get access to be able to swim.”“This is why I’m so against New Parks clos­ing.”How does the council plan to support swimmers with complex disabilitiesLeicester City Council said it had spoken to a range of swimming pool users during the consultation to understand their individual requirements and explore whether their needs could be met at other sites.A council spokesperson said, "All city council swimming pools offer disabled pool hoists designed to support users with diverse mobility requirements and transfer preferences, including compatibility with standard slings and adapted poolside chairs.”"After speaking with Sue, we understand that her son needs deeper water, so Aylestone Leisure Centre is making some small adaptions that will mean this centre will also be suitable for them and others to use.”"No decision has been made on the future of New Parks Leisure Centre, and we encourage everyone to have their say by November 3rd."You use AI every day.
